deep.reconstruction:
NOTATION. In Lamé's notation, Delta^2 means the ordinary Laplacian Δ = ∂xx+∂yy+∂zz; it is not the bilaplacian. λ and μ are Lamé's constants. N1 = λθ + 2μ u_x is the normal stress on planes x = const. T3 = μ(u_y+v_x) and T2 = μ(u_z+w_x) are the shear stresses on those planes. θ = div(u,v,w). The previous page cites Poggendorff's Annalen (dated Febr. 1856). The next page continues with the same stresses N1, T2, T3 for a body bounded by the plane x = 0. The page is a study of the elastic half-space x > 0 with tractions on x = 0, using a single potential χ.

(1) Displacement representation:
 u = (λ+μ)χ_xx − (λ+2μ)Δχ,
 v = (λ+μ)χ_xy,
 w = (λ+μ)χ_xz.
[My fill-in] θ = (λ+μ)Δχ_x − (λ+2μ)Δχ_x = −μΔχ_x. Navier's equations (λ+μ)∇θ + μΔ(u,v,w) = 0 then give 0 for the y and z components and −μ(λ+2μ)ΔΔχ for the x component. So the representation solves the homogeneous elastostatic equations exactly when χ is biharmonic. In modern terms this is a Galerkin vector (equivalently a Love strain function) with only one component, χ e_x, up to normalisation and sign. It gives the part of the general solution with zero 'twist': the next page's γ = ∫(∂T2/∂y − ∂T3/∂z)dx vanishes identically for it.

(2) Stresses, integrated in x. The transcription reads 1/x; the prefactor should be 1/μ. Put h = Δχ.
 (1/μ)∫N1 dx = −λh + 2(λ+μ)χ_xx − 2(λ+2μ)h = 2(λ+μ)χ_xx − (3λ+4μ)h. This is correct.
 For the shear stresses, T3/μ = ∂y[2(λ+μ)χ_xx − (λ+2μ)h] and T2/μ = ∂z[same]. Hence (1/μ)∫T3 dy = (1/μ)∫T2 dz = 2(λ+μ)χ_xx − (λ+2μ)h. Riemann struck out the '+' between the two integrals, so the intended reading is equality of the two. He writes the coefficient as (λ+3μ); the correct value is (λ+2μ). Either this is a misreading of the handwriting or a slip.

(3) Key construction: harmonic combinations. Riemann forms
 q = (λ+μ)(x h_x − 2χ_xx) + c_q h, with boundary condition q = 0 at x = 0;
 p = (λ+μ)(x h_x − 2χ_xx) + c_p h, with boundary condition ∂p/∂x = 0 at x = 0.
[My fill-in] Since χ is biharmonic, h is harmonic. Then Δ(x h_x) = 2h_xx and Δχ_xx = h_xx, so every E_c = (λ+μ)(x h_x − 2χ_xx) + c·h is harmonic.
 At x = 0, E_c = −2(λ+μ)χ_xx + c h. With c_q = λ+2μ, q|_{x=0} = −(1/μ)∫T2 dz. So 'q = 0 on x = 0' is the condition of no shear traction.
 Also ∂E_c/∂x at x = 0 equals (λ+μ+c)h_x − 2(λ+μ)χ_xxx, while −N1/μ = (3λ+4μ)h_x − 2(λ+μ)χ_xxx. So with c_p = 2λ+3μ, ∂p/∂x|_{x=0} = −N1/μ, and 'p_x = 0 on x = 0' is the condition of no normal traction. Riemann indeed uses 2λ+3μ in the following lines. The p-line coefficient itself is written ambiguously (λ + 2(λ+..μ)).
 The idea is that the boundary data for the stresses become Dirichlet data for one harmonic function q and Neumann data for another, p. The difference p − q = (c_p − c_q)h eliminates the x-terms and returns Δχ. Then the q-equation gives χ_xx.

(4) Riemann writes p' − q' = 2(λ+μ)Δχ' = p + q and introduces a second potential χ' with Δχ' = χ. He then tries the symmetric pair
 (λ+μ)Δχ' = (λ+μ)(x h_x − 2χ_xx) + (2λ+3μ)h,
 (λ+μ)Δχ = (λ+μ)(xΔχ'_x − 2χ'_xx) + (2λ+3μ)Δχ'.
Rewriting with Δχ' = χ gives the line (λ+μ)(xχ_x − 4χ'_xx) + (λ+3μ)χ = q, where '∇q' is probably 'q' or '2q'.
He substitutes one relation into the other: x∂x(x h_x − 2χ_xx), etc. Combining, he arrives at a coefficient [(λ+μ) − (2λ+3μ)²/(λ+μ)]Δχ. He simplifies this to (3λ+4μ)(λ+2μ)/(λ+μ)·Δχ.
[Check] (λ+μ)² − (2λ+3μ)² = −(λ+2μ)(3λ+4μ). The correct value is −(3λ+4μ)(λ+2μ)/(λ+μ), so a minus sign is missing.

(5) Final recovery formula. From the definition of q' with coefficient λ+3μ:
 2χ'_xx = xΔχ'_x + (λ+3μ)/(λ+μ)·Δχ' − q'/(λ+μ). This follows correctly.
 He then substitutes Δχ' = (p+q)/(2(λ+μ)):
 = x∂x(p+q)/(2(λ+μ)) + (λ+3μ)(p+q)/(2(λ+μ)²) + q/(λ+μ).
The last term follows if q' = −q, consistent with 'p' − q' = p + q', i.e. p' = p and q' = −q. Otherwise it is a sign or prime slip.

Overall: a sketch of the Boussinesq–Cerruti-type traction problem for the half-space. It uses a biharmonic one-component Galerkin potential and reduces the problem to harmonic functions with Dirichlet and Neumann data on the boundary plane. The work is exploratory, with several coefficient and sign slips, and is unfinished.
errors: The prefactor transcribed as 1/x in front of ∫N1 dx and the shear integrals must be 1/μ for the right-hand sides to be correct.
(1/μ)∫T3 dy = (1/μ)∫T2 dz equals 2(λ+μ)χ_xx − (λ+2μ)Δχ. The page shows −(λ+3μ)Δχ, so either this is a misreading or a coefficient slip (λ+3μ instead of λ+2μ).

The relation p' − q' = 2(λ+μ)Δχ' does not match the coefficients as written. With c_p = 2λ+3μ and c_q = λ+3μ (or λ+2μ), p − q equals λΔχ (or (λ+μ)Δχ), not 2(λ+μ)Δχ. The coefficients are evidently in flux.
Sign slip: (λ+μ) − (2λ+3μ)²/(λ+μ) = −(3λ+4μ)(λ+2μ)/(λ+μ); Riemann omits the minus sign.
In the last line, −q'/(λ+μ) is replaced by +q/(λ+μ). This is correct only under the implicit convention q' = −q.
The line '(λ+μ)(x∂Δ²χ/∂x + 2∂²χ/∂x² − 4∂²χ/∂x²)' is an unfinished fragment. Its relation to the surrounding lines is unclear.

results.what: Representation u = (λ+μ)χ_xx − (λ+2μ)Δχ, v = (λ+μ)χ_xy, w = (λ+μ)χ_xz, which solves the Navier equations iff ΔΔχ = 0
results.modern_name: Galerkin vector with one component / Love strain function (Boussinesq–Galerkin representation)
results.usually_credited_to: Galerkin (1930); Love (1906, axisymmetric strain function); related potentials in Boussinesq (1885)

results.what: Computation of the stresses N1, T2, T3 on planes x = const in terms of χ, and of their x-, y- and z-integrals
results.modern_name: Stress components from the Galerkin potential

results.what: Combinations (λ+μ)(xΔχ_x − 2χ_xx) + cΔχ are harmonic. On x = 0 they encode zero shear traction (Dirichlet data) and zero normal traction (Neumann data), reducing the half-space traction problem to harmonic functions
results.modern_name: Reduction of the Boussinesq–Cerruti half-space problem to harmonic potentials (Papkovich–Neuber/Boussinesq style x·∂h/∂x terms)

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann is not known to have worked on 3D elastostatics. A single biharmonic potential generating Navier solutions (the one-component Galerkin vector / Love strain function) is credited to Boussinesq, Love and Galerkin decades later. The same holds for its use to reduce the half-space traction problem to harmonic boundary-value problems. Finding this around 1856 would be a notable unpublished detail. However, the page is fragmentary, the computations are unfinished and slip-ridden, and Lamé–Clapeyron, Kelvin and others had related half-space methods earlier. So a major-priority claim is not warranted.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x,y,z,l,m=symbols('x y z lambda mu'); c=Function('chi')(x,y,z); L=lambda f: diff(f,x,2)+diff(f,y,2)+diff(f,z,2); u=(l+m)*diff(c,x,2)-(l+2*m)*L(c); v=(l+m)*diff(c,x,y); w=(l+m)*diff(c,x,z); th=diff(u,x)+diff(v,y)+diff(w,z); simplify(th + m*diff(L(c),x))

checkable.asserts: The Navier equations reduce to −μ(λ+2μ)ΔΔχ = 0 in x and are identically satisfied in y and z, so χ must be biharmonic (results 0, 0, 0)
The twist combination ∂T2/∂y − ∂T3/∂z vanishes for this potential (result 0)
ΔE = (λ+μ)xΔh_x + cΔh, so E is harmonic whenever χ is biharmonic (result 0)
With c_q = λ+2μ, q at x = 0 equals −(1/μ)∫T2 dz (result 0)
Equals −(λ+2μ)(3λ+4μ), so the page's coefficient should carry a minus sign

transcription_corrections: '1/x ∫N1 dx' and '1/x ∫T3 dy' should read '1/μ ∫…' (the prefactor is μ, not x).
Δ² throughout is Lamé's notation for the Laplacian, not the bilaplacian.
In the shear line the struck '+' suggests '(1/μ)∫T3 dy = (1/μ)∫T2 dz = …' (an equality of the two integrals), not a sum.
The coefficient read as (λ+3μ) in the shear and q lines may be (λ+2μ) in the hand; mathematically it should be λ+2μ for the shear integral.
'= ∇q' in the line (λ+μ)(x∂χ/∂x − 4∂²χ'/∂x²) + (λ+3μ)χ is probably '= q' or '= 2q'; there is no nabla operator here.
'x=0, q=0' and 'x=0, ∂p/∂x=0' are boundary conditions on the plane x = 0 (written to the right of the q- and p-lines).
The final simplified coefficient on the page is (3λ+4μ)(λ+2μ)/(λ+μ); it is written without the required minus sign.
